Basis: the civil-code article that makes the debtor liable in damages for non-performance or delay unless he proves a foreign cause (impossibility not due to him); check the exact paragraph and the exception for a cause beyond his control.
Binding force of the contract and good-faith performance (civil-code articles on the effects of the contract): supporting grounds, not a cause of action on their own.
Element to prove: a valid contract binding both parties, its date, its object and the obligation the defendant undertook (sale, works contract, transport, lease or other).
Element to prove: the breach - late performance, failure to deliver, stoppage or defective performance of works, or another contractual breach by the defendant; the date the performance was due.
Element to prove: the damage suffered (loss incurred and profit lost) and its amount; whether the damage was foreseeable at the time of contracting, absent fraud or gross fault.
Element to prove: the causal link between the breach and the damage (damage being the natural result of the breach, not avoidable by reasonable effort).
Burden of proof: the creditor proves the obligation; the debtor proves its performance or the foreign cause that excuses him (civil-code proof rules - import the proof module).

Formal notice (iedhar) before damages: damages are due only after the debtor is put on notice, unless the law or the contract dispenses with it; check the exceptions (performance impossible or useless through the debtor's act, tort compensation, return of stolen or unduly received thing, debtor's written refusal) - import formal-notice.
Form and means of the notice: a bailiff's warning or an equivalent writ, or by post as the law allows; the date it was served; served before the petition is filed.

Is a delay damage for a sum of money (interest-like) excluded or regulated differently? Check civil-code rules on delay damages for money obligations and the prohibition of interest between individuals.

Assessment of damages: the court assesses when the contract or the law does not fix them; loss suffered and profit lost; foreseeability limit in contract; liability for fraud or gross fault extends to unforeseeable damage.

Agreed damages (penalty clause): if the contract fixes the compensation, it is due unless the debtor proves no damage; the judge may reduce it if excessive or if partly performed; increase only for fraud or gross fault.
Clauses excluding or limiting liability: void for fraud or gross fault; check before relying on a clause.
Creditor's own fault and duty to mitigate: the judge may reduce or refuse damages where the creditor contributed to the damage.

Limitation: the general fifteen-year limitation for contractual obligations, counted from the day the debt became due; shorter periods for periodic rights (rent - five years), professional fees and trader supplies (one or two years); limitation is not raised by the court of its own motion - import periods.

Special limitation periods by contract type: carrier liability (transport contract - commercial code short period), works contract decennial liability of architect and contractor and the period to bring that claim, hidden defects in sale (one year from delivery); check that the claim is not really one of these.
Competent section: the civil section of the tribunal (or the commercial section if the dispute is commercial; the real-property section for some leases of premises) - import court-sections.

Territorial jurisdiction: the defendant's domicile as the rule; in contract matters, the court where the contract was concluded or performed may also be competent; a jurisdiction clause is valid only between traders - import territorial-jurisdiction.

Exits from the ordinary courts: a public administrative body as party (administrative courts, administrative contracts / public procurement); the specialised commercial court for its listed matters with prior conciliation; the criminal judge when the damage results from an offence; an order to pay for a fixed written debt - import ordinary-court-exits.
Conciliation before the specialised commercial court and the record of non-conciliation to attach where that court is competent - import conciliation-mediation.

Petition formalities: court, parties' identities, legal person details, brief facts, requests and grounds, list of documents, signature, Arabic, fees, standing and interest, capacity and representation (Code of civil and administrative procedure) - import petition-formal-elements.

Land registry publication: if the contract concerns real property rights (for example a lease or sale of real property with a published deed), check whether the petition must be published - import land-registry-publication.
Boundary: rescission of the contract with damages is a different claim (rescission requests); this claim asks damages without rescission.
Boundary: tortious liability (harm outside a contract) is a different claim; no cumulation of contractual and tortious liability between contracting parties.
Boundary: a claim for payment of the price, rent or wages (performance of a money obligation) is a different claim; delay damages on a sum of money follow special rules.
Boundary: guarantee against hidden defects or eviction in sale, and the contractor's decennial liability, have their own rules and periods.
Boundary: labour contract breaches go to the social section after labour conciliation; commercial lease disputes follow the commercial code.

Request: damages for loss suffered and profit lost, with the amount; supporting request for specific performance (execution in kind) where still possible, and a penalty payment (astreinte) to compel it.
Accessory requests: costs borne by the losing party; provisional execution only within the procedure code's conditions; penalty payment; import accessory-requests where available.

Documents: the contract (or proof of it), the formal notice record (bailiff's report or registered letter receipt), proof of the damage and its amount (invoices, expert report), proof of the breach (report, correspondence), translation into Arabic of foreign-language documents.
Proof of the contract: writing required above the statutory sum in civil matters; freedom of proof in commercial matters - import proof.
Expertise: the lawyer may ask the court for an expert to assess the damage; a request for expertise is not a substitute for stating the amount claimed.

Amendments to remember: the civil code reform of 2005 (law 05-10) touched several contract articles; the procedure code is law 08-09 as amended by law 22-13 (specialised commercial courts); check the version in force of each cited article.
